questions.prompt: What phase does S add to the |1> amplitude relative to |0>?
questions.explanation: S has diagonal entries 1 and i, and i=exp(i pi/2). The |0> amplitude is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which identity holds for the standard T gate?
questions.explanation: Two phase increments of pi/4 add to pi/2. This gives the diagonal matrix for S.

questions.prompt: In what units do the explicit Rx, Ry and Rz helpers take their angles?
questions.explanation: The rotation formulas use radians. A half turn is pi radians and a quarter turn is pi/2.

questions.prompt: Starting from |0>, what is P(1) after Ry(pi/2)?
questions.explanation: P(1)=sin squared(theta/2). At theta=pi/2, the half angle is pi/4 and its squared sine is 1/2.

questions.prompt: Starting from |0>, what is P(1) after Ry(pi)?
questions.explanation: The resulting amplitudes are cos(pi/2)=0 and sin(pi/2)=1. This rotation prepares |1>.

questions.prompt: Starting from |0>, what is P(0) after H, S, H?
questions.explanation: S inserts relative phase pi/2 between the two equal amplitudes. The final H gives P(0)=(1+cos(pi/2))/2=1/2.

questions.prompt: Starting from |0>, what is P(0) after H, T, H?
questions.explanation: Use relative phase pi/4 in the interference formula. P(0)=(1+1/sqrt(2))/2; approximately 0.146 is P(1).

questions.prompt: How do S and Rz(pi/2) compare as isolated gates?

options.text: They are identical matrices entry by entry
They have opposite Z measurement probabilities for every input
They differ by a global phase, so isolated-state predictions agree
One is unitary and the other is not

questions.explanation: Rz(pi/2) has diagonal phases exp(-i pi/4) and exp(i pi/4). Factoring out exp(-i pi/4) leaves S.

questions.prompt: Ry(2 pi) multiplies a statevector by -1. What does this imply for an isolated qubit?

options.text: It necessarily creates a mixed state
Its physical state and measurement probabilities are unchanged

questions.explanation: The same factor -1 multiplies every amplitude. This is global phase, not a relative phase or a bit flip.

questions.prompt: Why should controlled versions of two globally equivalent gates not automatically be treated as identical?

options.text: The phase can become relative between the control-0 and control-1 branches
A control removes all phase information
Controlled gates cannot act on superpositions
Every global phase becomes a probability

questions.explanation: The control-0 branch does nothing, while the control-1 branch applies the gate. A phase present only in the second branch can affect interference between them.
